questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] a per-tenant generated schema as a public API contract (mastertwenty, twenty/fabledocs3/adr-006-generated-graphql-single-pipeline.md). Scenario: the CRM opens an integration marketplace. About 3,000 integrations (Zapier zaps, partner apps with SDKs generated from introspection, customers' own sync scripts and webhook receivers) now hold API keys; a busy workspace has 40 of them; across the fleet admins rename, deactivate or delete roughly 150 fields and objects a day, usually without knowing who depends on them; and the business wants to price API volume by plan. Write your design before you look: what a field or object rename does to GraphQL clients, REST callers, generated SDKs and webhook receivers; how deactivating differs from deleting for an API consumer; how a schema that differs per workspace can still offer deprecation and versioning; how an integration learns that the schema changed; whether integrations register the operations they run; and how quotas are scoped and priced. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] A rename breaks clients in one step: each generated field is keyed by the field's current API name and carries only its type and description, with no deprecation flag and no entry under the old name, while the database side is an in-place column rename that keeps the data. Give renames a compatibility window in which the old name still resolves, marked deprecated, onto the same column.

[w3] A cosmetic relabel is an API rename: while label and API name are synchronised, which is the default for custom fields, the settings form recomputes the API name from every label edit, and the server merely checks that the two agree. Freeze the API name once a field has been used through the API, or show the admin which integrations will break before saving.

[w3] Writes that still use the old name fail outright: each key in the data is looked up among the object's current field and join-column names, and an unknown key throws an invalid-arguments error, so a zap writing the old field fails on every run. During the window, translate old names and log each use with the calling key, so owners can be told before the alias is removed.

[w2] Deactivation hides a field from the product, not from the API: schema generation takes every field of every object without looking at whether it is active, so a deactivated field is still served and still writable. That makes deactivation the natural deprecation stage: mark it deprecated in the API, measure who still uses it, and only then allow deletion.

[w3] Deletion is immediate and blind to consumers: the field's columns are dropped with cascade and its metadata row removed, and nothing looks for webhook subscriptions, workflows or recent API traffic that use it. The settings page offers deletion only for a deactivated field, but the server does not require it and there is no waiting period: require it server-side, block or warn when any key used the field recently, and keep a restorable copy for a grace period.

[w3] A per-workspace schema cannot carry one global version, but it already has a per-workspace one: send the workspace's metadata version on every response and in the published REST description, whose version is a fixed string today. The existing schema-version header check only runs after a request has already failed validation, on a path record operations never take, so it does not warn integrations either.

[w2] Registered operations make change impact knowable: there is no persisted-query support (only two unused error codes name it), so the platform cannot tell which fields an integration reads. If marketplace apps register their operations per key, a rename can list exactly the integrations it breaks, and the registry doubles as an allow-list.

[w2] Quotas belong to keys inside a workspace cap: today one pair of token buckets per workspace is shared by every API key, each operation costs one token whatever it returns, the limits are one server-wide setting (100 a second and 100 a minute by default), and API calls are never metered for billing. Give each key its own bucket under a workspace ceiling, weight cost by rows returned, and meter per plan.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the marketplace's first quarter. On a Monday an admin relabels 'Phone' to 'Mobile phone' and 40 integrations break in different ways; one customer's nightly import script starts at 02:00 and every other integration in that workspace gets rate-limited until it finishes; a custom object is renamed from Deal to Opportunity and Zapier triggers on new deals simply stop firing; a partner app built on last month's generated SDK reports errors nobody can explain; and every receiver that copied the documented signature check rejects every webhook. What breaks, how does each show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The relabel renamed the API field, so reads fail validation, writes fail on the unknown key, and webhook receivers quietly get records keyed by the new name, since the payload is the record keyed by current field names with no version marker. The compatibility window, frozen API names and a payload that identifies fields stably prevent all three.

[w3] One script starved the workspace because every key draws from the same workspace bucket and a bulk read costs the same single token as a lookup; per-key buckets, cost by rows and a separate lane for bulk jobs keep one integration from exhausting the others.

[w3] The triggers died silently because webhook subscriptions are plain strings matched exactly against the object's current singular name, and nothing validates them or rewrites them when an object is renamed. Subscribe by object id, or rewrite subscriptions as part of the rename and tell their owners.

[w2] A generated SDK is a snapshot of one workspace's schema at one moment, and record operations are executed before the server's validation step, so the partner sees field errors instead of a 'schema changed' signal. Emit the metadata version with every response and point integrations at the metadata change events, which already carry before-and-after diffs, so they can regenerate on purpose.

[w2] The documented signature recipe does not match the server: it encodes the payload as JSON twice before signing, and it presents the nonce header as replay protection although the nonce is not part of the signed string. Test the published examples against the real signer, and sign the nonce if receivers are told to rely on it.
[w1] You notice through per-key error rates by error code, lined up against the metadata change feed: a jump in invalid-argument errors minutes after a field update is a rename breaking someone.
keyPoints.quote: is the entire compatibility mechanism, which is a documented weakness of this ADR

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your contract design against the alternatives: renaming immediately versus compatibility windows with deprecated aliases versus API names that never change once created; one global API version versus a per-workspace schema version versus no versioning plus a change feed; registered operations versus open queries for any key holder; per-key quotas priced by cost versus one shared workspace quota; and versioned webhook payloads keyed by stable ids versus unversioned payloads. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Immediate renames keep the schema honest and cost every consumer a break; aliases with a deadline cost two names per field for a while and a cleanup job, but turn breaks into scheduled migrations; immutable API names never break anyone, at the price of API names that stop matching what users see on screen.

[w3] A global version cannot describe a schema each tenant edits at runtime; a per-workspace version tells a client exactly when its snapshot went stale but promises nothing about what changed; a change feed of metadata events says what changed, field by field, and is cheap because the events already exist, at the cost of every integration having to subscribe and react.

[w2] Registered operations give impact analysis, an allow-list and cacheable query plans, at the cost of friction for ad-hoc scripts and a registration flow; open queries keep exploration easy, and any key holder can introspect the workspace's schema, which is exactly why nobody knows who uses what.

[w2] Per-key quotas priced by cost are fair and sellable, at the cost of a metering pipeline the billing side does not have for API traffic; one workspace bucket charging per operation is trivial to run but lets one integration starve the rest and prices a thousand-row export like a single lookup.

[w2] Versioned payloads keyed by stable ids survive renames and let receivers upgrade on their own schedule, at the cost of a translation layer and a version to maintain; name-keyed, unversioned payloads are readable and simple, and every rename becomes a silent contract change.

keyPoints.text: [w1] Requiring deactivation before deletion adds a step for admins and buys an observation period in which nothing is lost; today deactivation is a UI step only, since through the API an active field deletes at once, which is convenient and irreversible because the column goes with it.
